title: PC Parts Compatibility
summary: Guide PC builders toward compatible parts using catalog attributes, category rules and explicit vendor exceptions.
narrative:
Design a service for the assemble-a-PC section of the Newegg website, where customers pick the different parts of a PC and learn whether those parts are compatible. Keep track of compatibility across selections, explain conflicts, and filter the next category to compatible candidates. This is primarily a frontend and database design problem; auto parts fitment is a related application.

Store ~500 K parts across ~12 categories in SQL, with attributes including CPU socket, RAM type, form factor, TDP and PSU wattage. Use a small rules table per category pair: motherboard.socket = cpu.socket, total TDP × 1.5 ≤ psu.watts, and the case must support the board form factor. Avoid an N² pair matrix; keep explicit known-incompatible and verified-compatible vendor pairs in an exceptions table. Saved builds are SQL rows keyed by build id, exposed through shareable URLs.

About 2 M builder sessions/day × ~20 picks produce ~40 M filter queries/day, or ~460/s with ~2 K/s peaks. Route clients through a Load Balancer to redundant Web Servers. Filter candidates using Search Index attributes, cache candidate lists and validation results per selection, and validate the entire build server-side on every change and at checkout. Catalog and rule changes are only thousands/day: publish admin change events to a Message Queue, then let a Worker read SQL, re-index affected parts and invalidate Cache. Optionally serve product images and the builder UI through a CDN and monitor index freshness.

functional: Filter the next part category as selections change and explain incompatible combinations
Store parts, category attributes, category-pair rules, vendor exceptions and saved builds in SQL
Use Search Index attribute filters and cache compatible candidates and validation results per selection
Validate the full build server-side on every change and checkout; apply vendor exceptions explicitly
Publish catalog/rule changes from the admin API; have a Worker read SQL, re-index parts and invalidate affected cache entries
nonFunctional: Serve ~460 filter queries/s on average and ~2 K/s at peak
Keep the builder available after one Web Server failure
Precompute common compatibility checks and tolerate briefly stale suggestions while validating against current rules at checkout
constraints: Clients must not access SQL directly; Search Index access must pass through Web Servers
Use category-pair attribute rules plus explicit exceptions instead of an N² compatibility matrix
Keep Search Index connected to a Worker that applies catalog changes
Check CPU socket and RAM type, total TDP × 1.5 ≤ PSU watts, and case/board form factor
capacity: 2 M sessions/day × ~20 picks ≈ 40 M filter queries/day ≈ 460/s; ~2 K/s peak
Catalog updates: thousands/day, far below filter traffic
specs.tradeoff: Attribute rules avoid a quadratic compatibility matrix and support fast search filters, but vendor-specific exceptions still need explicit records. Asynchronous indexing and caching improve browsing speed at the cost of stale suggestions; authoritative server validation catches conflicts before checkout.
specs.bonus: Connect Client → CDN for product images and the builder UI, and add Monitoring for stale indexes and invalidation failures.

topologyRules.message: Clients access parts and saved builds through the Web Server, never directly from SQL.
Candidate searches must pass through the Web Server for selection validation.

resilienceRules.message: Run at least two Web Servers so a failure does not interrupt the builder.
The index must be kept in sync with the catalog by a Worker.

hints: Start with Client → Load Balancer → Web Server → SQL Database. Model part attributes, category-pair rules, explicit exceptions and saved builds; validate each complete selection on the server.

Connect Web Server → Search Index for attribute-filtered candidates and → Cache for reusable candidate lists. Send admin changes through Web Server → Message Queue → Worker; connect the Worker to SQL, Search Index and Cache.

Run two Web Servers, each connected to SQL, Search Index, Cache and Message Queue. The Worker reads SQL, updates Search Index and invalidates Cache. Add Client → CDN for images/UI and Web Server → Monitoring.
tips: Auto parts compatibility is another way to describe this problem.
Presumably, you might have a compatibility list for each part provided. Narrow down the problem to a particular type of part.
This problem is more about frontend and DB design than about distributed systems.
Keep track of each part's compatibility with other parts, so the customer is told when two parts they picked are not compatible.
